title: Seeing God
hook: Catholic and Orthodox writers speak of seeing God face to face as our joy
tomorrow: Not as those without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, new creation: the holy city coming down, not souls floating up. Your line was heaven comes down. What piece of the earth did you care for? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

Hold up a spoon and look into the bowl of it. There you are, upside down, blurred, the color off. It's you, but not clearly. Paul reaches for a picture like that when he writes to Corinth about what comes at the end: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." Behind that line stands an old refusal. Moses, who had seen the burning bush and the sea split open, once asked God, "I beseech thee, shew me thy glory." And God answered, "Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live." Today's word is the name one tradition gives to the seeing Paul hopes for.

First, the refusal. God sets Moses in a cleft of the rock, covers him with a hand while the glory passes by, and then lets him see from behind. Not the face. Moses has to be hidden to be kept safe. Second, the promise. Jesus says, "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God." The letter of John says, "we shall see him as he is." And Paul's glass, in the King James, is a mirror. Some readers say God is glimpsed now only in reflections: in scripture, in other people, in a sunset, never straight on. Then, face to face. Third, the name. Catholic theology calls this the beatific vision, from the Latin for the seeing that makes blessed. The idea is that seeing God isn't a reward handed out in heaven alongside other rewards. It is the joy itself. Thomas Aquinas, among others, taught that human longing finally comes to rest there. Orthodox writers speak in their own way, of beholding the light of God, the light the disciples saw on the mountain when Jesus was transfigured, and of sharing in God's life. Protestant hymns sing of seeing Christ face to face. The churches don't simply use different words here; they have argued about it. Orthodox theology holds that God's essence stays beyond any creature, and the saints see and share God's uncreated light; Catholic theology speaks of seeing God's essence. Both place the joy in seeing God. Fourth, the seeing goes both ways. Paul finishes his sentence: "then shall I know even as also I am known." In Paul's line, being known comes first. The seeing comes after.

Here's the practice: a minute with the face you long to see. Settle, and breathe. Close your eyes. If you pray, you can bring to mind the hope of seeing God's face, without trying to picture any features, only the sense of being looked at with love, and of looking back. If you don't pray, you can bring to mind the face of someone who has loved you well, and let yourself be seen by it. Either way, don't perform. Just be seen. The bell holds the time.
Beatific vision. From the Latin, the seeing that makes blessed: the hope of seeing God face to face, as the joy itself.
Your line: face to face. Today, give one person your full face: put the phone down, turn toward them, and look while they talk. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching names the vision of God as the final happiness of the saints; Orthodox prayer and icons speak of beholding the uncreated light; Protestant hymns and sermons speak of seeing Christ face to face.

fork.setup: you're Moses. you've seen a burning bush, a split sea and fire on the mountain. you ask God to show you his glory. what does God do?
options: shows you his face at once.
hides you in the rock and lets you see from behind.
fork.reveal: God covers Moses with his hand as the glory passes, then lets him see from behind. Christians read the face as saved for the end of the story.

original.note: Latin: the vision that makes blessed, the name Catholic theology gives to seeing God.

trapdoor: what you thought: heaven is a nice place, and seeing God is part of the tour.
what it means: Christians hope to see God face to face, and in Catholic teaching that seeing is the joy itself.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 33's 'no man shall see me, and live' set beside 1 Corinthians 13's 'then face to face,' and the Latin visio beatifica.
